Kawasaki Disease

CRASH and Burn criteria · incomplete disease · intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin within 10 days · echocardiogram · mimics · coronary complicationsHas fever lasted 5 days with 4 criteria, and is the child still inside the 10-day window?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Fever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 CRASH criteria is Kawasaki disease; with only 2 or 3, check C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) for incomplete disease.
  • Give IVIG plus high-dose aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset; obtain an echocardiogram at diagnosis without delaying treatment.
  • Sterile pyuria is part of the disease; aspirin is given despite the usual rule against aspirin in children.
What it is

Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome): a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries.

Driver

Immune-mediated arteritis; the cause is unknown.

Triggers

None proven. Age under 5, peak 6 to 24 months

non-modifiable

; Asian, especially Japanese, ancestry

non-modifiable

Chain

Inflamed medium-sized arteries, mainly the coronaries

the coronary wall dilates into an aneurysm

the aneurysm expands, ruptures or thromboses

ischemia, infarction or heart failure

Insights

Untreated, about 25% have some coronary artery involvement; treatment cuts coronary aneurysms from 20% to under 5%.

Aneurysms form after the first week, so heart failure can arrive weeks after an untreated, self-limited illness.

Days 1 to 2nonexudative conjunctivitis
By day 5rash and red lips; 5 days of fever opens the criteria
Day 10target for IVIG; peeling at the nails begins

Weeks to monthscoronary aneurysm, infarction, heart failure
2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
Fast breathing, fast pulse, low blood pressure and a big heart weeks after a Kawasaki illnessHeart failure from coronary disease: obtain an electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiography now.
Infant with fever and fewer than 4 criteria (step 5 gives the age and fever rule)Evaluate for incomplete disease now; infants under 1 year still develop aneurysms.
Shock with vomiting or diarrhea weeks after COVID-19Consider MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) rather than Kawasaki disease.
3Differential
Kawasaki mimics
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Scarlet feverSandpaper rash, Pastia lines and no conjunctivitis; both can show a strawberry tongue.Rapid strep test; throat culture if negative.
AdenovirusExudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis; Kawasaki conjunctivitis is nonexudative.Send viral testing on a throat or eye swab.
MeaslesUnvaccinated, cough and coryza, Koplik spots, rash spreading from the face down.Measles antibody serology or viral testing.
MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children)Weeks after COVID-19, older child, prominent GI symptoms and shock.COVID-19 test or antibodies with the clinical criteria.
Toxic shock syndromeHypotension with multiorgan failure; desquamation later.Support the circulation and apply the clinical criteria; cultures are often negative.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysisDrug exposure, target lesions, mucosal erosions and ulcers.Stop the drug; skin biopsy when unclear.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndromePerioral crusting; Nikolsky sign positive.Diagnose clinically.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
High fever, red eyes, red swollen hands, nodes and cracked lips that cleared on their ownAn earlier, untreated Kawasaki illnessLook for coronary disease: ECG and echocardiography.
Temperature 38 C two months laterLow grade, not a new episodeObtain ECG and echocardiography for the complication.
No murmurArgues against mitral stenosis; Kawasaki disease causes mitral regurgitationTreat as heart failure from coronary disease; obtain echocardiography.
No raised jugular venous pressure or pulsus paradoxusArgues against tamponadeObtain echocardiography, which also shows any effusion.
Cardiomegaly and ST depression in leads II and IIIIschemic heart failureEchocardiography now.
Urinalysis: many white cells, no bacteriaSterile pyuria from the disease itselfContinue IVIG and aspirin.
Pause point
Fewer than four criteria, coronary dilation or aneurysm on echocardiography Offered: waiting for a fourth criterion A fourth criterion is not required → Start IVIG
5Diagnostic criteria
CRASH and Burn
CriterionFeature
ConjunctivitisBilateral, nonexudative, limbal sparing
RashPolymorphous, perineal accentuation
AdenopathyCervical, at least 1.5 cm, usually a single node; the least common criterion
Strawberry tongueOr cracked red lips; no ulcers, no exudate
Hands and feetErythema and edema; periungual peeling in weeks 2 to 3
BurnFever 5 days or more
Rules
DiagnosisRequires
Kawasaki diseaseFever 5 days or more plus at least 4 criteria
Incomplete diseaseFever 5 days or more with 2 or 3 criteria
Infant: evaluate for incomplete diseaseInfant 6 months or younger with fever 7 days or more and no other explanation
6Severity
Coronary result and response
FindingMeaning
No coronary change on follow-up echocardiographyAspirin may be stopped once ESR and platelets normalize (step 7 gives the timing)
Coronary aneurysmAspirin continues indefinitely
Giant aneurysm, over 8 mmGreatest risk; added anticoagulant therapy may be needed
Fever persisting 36 h after IVIGIVIG resistance: a second dose (step 7); higher aneurysm risk
7Treatment
1

Diagnosis madeWithin 10 days of fever onset

IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin.

2

After day 10Seen after day 10

Give IVIG when fever without another cause or coronary changes continue, with a raised CRP or ESR.

3

AfebrileFever gone

Step down to low-dose aspirin until follow-up echocardiography, at least 8 weeks after onset. Aspirin is given for its antithrombotic effect; the usual rule against aspirin in children does not apply here.

4

IVIG resistanceFever persisting 36 h after IVIG

Second IVIG dose; steroids or infliximab are alternatives.

8Follow-up
After treatment
SituationDo
Uncomplicated diseaseEchocardiography at diagnosis, repeated 1 to 2 weeks after treatment and again at 4 to 6 weeks AnKing counts from onset: at 1 to 2 weeks and at 6 to 8 weeks after onset.
Fast breathing or irritability weeks laterECG and echocardiogram
Live vaccines after IVIGGenerally defer MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella 11 months
On long-term aspirinAnnual influenza vaccine
Practice
  1. 4-year-old boy brought in on day 12 of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands since the first week; CRP 12 mg/dL → IVIG now → give IVIG even beyond day 10 when unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESR
  2. 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasingly fast breathing and irritability; 2 months earlier he had a high fever, red eyes, cracked red lips, enlarged lymph nodes and red swollen hands, all of which cleared without treatment within 14 days; in obvious discomfort; T 38 C (100.4 F); HR 150/min; RR 60/min; BP 60/40 mm Hg; the rest of the examination is normal; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly; ECG: ST-segment depression in leads II and III, left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation → Congestive heart failure → late cardiac complication of untreated Kawasaki disease: cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression, and no murmur or signs of tamponade
  3. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.5 C; bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge; strawberry tongue; a polymorphous rash; edema of both hands; one cervical lymph node 1.8 cm → Kawasaki disease → fever 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 criteria; IVIG plus aspirin
  4. 4-year-old boy with 5 days of fever; T 39.0 C; only 3 of the 5 criteria are present: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips and a polymorphous rash; echocardiogram shows coronary artery dilation → IVIG and aspirin now → incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on the coronary finding
  5. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and sore throat; T 39.4 C; exudative pharyngitis; strawberry tongue; a fine sandpaper-like rash, densest in the skin creases; no conjunctivitis → Scarlet fever → a positive rapid strep test confirms it; penicillin
  6. 4-year-old boy who is unvaccinated; 4 days of fever, cough and runny nose; T 39.8 C; bilateral conjunctivitis; Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa; a red rash that began on the face and is spreading downward → Measles → Koplik spots and a descending rash decide it; measles antibody serology confirms
  7. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands; IVIG and aspirin are ordered; urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no bacteria → Continue IVIG and aspirin as planned → sterile pyuria is Kawasaki urethritis, a feature of the disease, not a second diagnosis
  8. 9-year-old boy with 3 days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, 4 weeks after COVID-19; T 39.5 C; HR 168/min; BP 70/40 mm Hg; a diffuse red rash; cool hands and feet; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; troponin raised → Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children → weeks after COVID-19, with prominent GI symptoms and shock
  9. 3-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.4 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands → Echocardiogram → baseline coronary assessment at diagnosis; IVIG is not delayed for it
  10. 2-year-old girl, 3 weeks after 7 days of fever with conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and hand swelling that were never treated; afebrile now; peeling skin around the fingernails; platelet count 780,000/mm³ → Coronary artery aneurysm → echocardiogram now; untreated aneurysms can progress to infarction or heart failure
  11. 5-year-old girl who received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for Kawasaki disease; the infusion ended 40 hours ago; T 39.3 C; conjunctivitis and rash persist → Second dose of IVIG → fever persisting 36 h after IVIG defines resistance
  12. 3-year-old boy at a well visit 2 months after he was given IVIG 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease; afebrile; aspirin stopped after a normal echocardiogram; due for routine vaccines → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today → live vaccines are deferred 11 months after IVIG; inactivated vaccines are not
  13. 6-year-old boy treated with IVIG and aspirin for Kawasaki disease; afebrile since the day after the infusion; echocardiogram at diagnosis normal → Repeat echocardiogram at 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks → coronary changes can appear after a normal first study
How NBME framed it The untreated Kawasaki illness sits in the past history as an episode that resolved on its own, and the mechanism lead-in is keyed to heart failure. The criteria appear in lay words ("pink eye," swollen hands) and are never named.
Distractors: NBME question
True-fact-wrong-slotPericardial effusion: a real Kawasaki complication, but tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus; cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression fits heart failure.
Unchecked attributeMitral valve obstruction: Kawasaki affects the mitral valve as regurgitation, not stenosis, and no stenotic murmur is heard.
Salient decoyChronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease: Kawasaki rarely involves the lungs, and the film shows cardiomegaly rather than interstitial fibrosis.
Class-vs-memberThickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles: Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries and rarely involves the pulmonary vessels.
Pairs with Heart Failure in a Child: is the failing heart from an untreated Kawasaki illness in the history or from an acute viral myocarditis?
Transferable rules

A candidate diagnosis that explains only a subset of the findings is wrong. With sterile pyuria, a UTI (urinary tract infection) explains only the fever and the urine white cells; Kawasaki disease explains all the findings. Check which findings a diagnosis leaves unexplained.
